📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iraqi National Security Adviser Qasim al-Aboudi says that Iraq remains committed to the joint security agreement between Baghdad and Tehran.

Al-Aboudi met with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Thursday in Baghdad, according to Lebanon’s Al-Mayadeen news network.
​
He said, “Iraq’s stability contributes to the stability of the region as a whole,” adding, “Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s government is committed to deepening ties with neighboring countries while expanding cooperation with the wider international community.”
​
Al-Aboudi further noted, “The Iraqi Constitution does not permit the presence of armed groups that threaten the security of other countries, and the government remains committed to ensuring that arms are held exclusively by the state.”
​
Ghalibaf, who arrived in Baghdad on Wednesday, met with several senior Iraqi officials, including his counterpart, Haibat al-Halbousi; President Nizar Mohammed Saeed Amidi; Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi; and the President of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Faiq Zaidan.

🏦🌴 Florida Democrats Buy a Message, Not the Candidate

Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist in the Florida legislature, beat Alex Vindman in the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate.

Vindman raised more than $16 million. Nixon raised about $975,000. He spent roughly $2.2 million on ads; she spent about $60,000. Nixon still won 56 percent to 44 percent. 

Vindman had the national donor network, a national security résumé, and the institutional support that usually comes with both. Nixon had a ground campaign, progressive backing, and a record of saying openly what many Democratic candidates try to reduce to a carefully reviewed statement.

A month after October 7, Nixon introduced a Florida resolution calling for a ceasefire in Israel and occupied Palestine. She has called for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel and made a point of saying she did not take AIPAC support. 

She was backed by progressive Democrats and allied groups, though the Democratic Socialists of America did not formally endorse her. 

Her victory does not mean Florida is about to elect a Democratic senator. Nixon now faces Republican Sen. Ashley Moody in a state where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2012. Moody remains the clear favorite. 

But the primary offered a more immediate result: Democratic voters rejected the candidate assembled by donors and party networks in favor of one who ran against the party’s preferred position on Gaza.

Vindman’s money was real. The endorsement machine was real. So was Nixon’s 56 percent.

The Democratic establishment keeps treating its left flank as a messaging problem. Florida just showed that it can also become a ballot problem.
